ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> These 20 adult speakers were recruited on the streets of downtown Chicago near Mindworks, a public-facing laboratory.

> We recruited 1338, 1165, and 1545 online participants using Prolific for the audiovisual, visual-only, and audio-only experiments, respectively.

> Each stimulus was viewed by about 40 participants, as prior work shows that memorability scores can be sufficiently calculated from 40 viewers (Isola et al., 2014; see Supplemental Table.2.1 for number of participants assigned to each speaker).

> For all online experiments in this study, participants were compensated an hourly rate of $8.00 and were allowed to end the experiment at any time.

> During the test phase that followed a page of test instructions, 18 stimuli from the same speaker (Speaker 1) were presented in 18 trials, and participants were asked to rate whether each stimulus was new or old on a 5-point Likert scale.

> Participants were not provided with any context for the speakers' explanations and were instructed to memorize the 9 stimuli for an upcoming memory test.

> Participants were told to press the r key when the border turned red.

> After the study phase, participants were shown instructions for the test phase, and their memory was tested using 18 old/new memory judgment test trials that included the 9 studied stimuli and 9 foil stimuli from the same speaker.

> In each test trial, the stimulus was presented in a looped manner, and the participant had to rate the stimulus as "definitely old," "probably old," "not sure," "probably new," or "definitely new."

> At the end of the second study-test block, participants filled out a demographic survey, rated whether the experiment ran smoothly, and gave additional comments, if any.

> We recruited a new group of 472 online participants on Prolific (221 female, 204 male, 27 other, see Supplemental Table.8.2 for age composition) and asked them to rate 12 attributes on a nine-point Likert scale (1=not at all,9=extremely) for gestures in each visual-only stimulus.

> Each trial (rating of 12 attributes on 1 visual-only stimulus) contained two attention check questions: (1) participants were asked to indicate a computer-generated random number between 1 and 9 (and were excluded if they answered any incorrectly), and (2) participants were asked whether the speaker in the video stimulus was wearing long sleeves (and were excluded if they answered more than half of the trials incorrectly).

> Before the 12 experimental trials, participants filled out a demographic survey.

> Not surprisingly (Revsine et al., 2025), participants were consistent in the stimuli they remembered when presented auditorily (Spearman-Brown corrected, SBc, ρ=.67, p<.001; Fig. 3B).

> But participants were also consistent in the stimuli they remembered when presented visually (SBc ρ=.49, p<.001, Fig. 3A) and audiovisually (SBc ρ=.59, p<.001, Fig. 3C).

> Between 32% and 45% of the recruited online participants were excluded, which aligns with current exclusion rates for online experiments.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: These 20 adult speakers were recruited on the streets of downtown Chicago near Mindworks, a public-facing laboratory.
We recruited 1338, 1165, and 1545 online participants using Prolific for the audiovisual, visual-only, and audio-only experiments, respectively.

Each stimulus was viewed by about 40 participants, as prior work shows that memorability scores can be sufficiently calculated from 40 viewers (Isola et al., 2014; see Supplemental Table.2.1 for number of participants assigned to each speaker).
For all online experiments in this study, participants were compensated an hourly rate of $8.00 and were allowed to end the experiment at any time.

During the test phase that followed a page of test instructions, 18 stimuli from the same speaker (Speaker 1) were presented in 18 trials, and participants were asked to rate whether each stimulus was new or old on a 5-point Likert scale.
Participants were not provided with any context for the speakers' explanations and were instructed to memorize the 9 stimuli for an upcoming memory test.
Participants were told to press the r key when the border turned red.

After the study phase, participants were shown instructions for the test phase, and their memory was tested using 18 old/new memory judgment test trials that included the 9 studied stimuli and 9 foil stimuli from the same speaker.
In each test trial, the stimulus was presented in a looped manner, and the participant had to rate the stimulus as "definitely old," "probably old," "not sure," "probably new," or "definitely new."
At the end of the second study-test block, participants filled out a demographic survey, rated whether the experiment ran smoothly, and gave additional comments, if any.

We recruited a new group of 472 online participants on Prolific (221 female, 204 male, 27 other, see Supplemental Table.8.2 for age composition) and asked them to rate 12 attributes on a nine-point Likert scale (1=not at all,9=extremely) for gestures in each visual-only stimulus.

Each trial (rating of 12 attributes on 1 visual-only stimulus) contained two attention check questions: (1) participants were asked to indicate a computer-generated random number between 1 and 9 (and were excluded if they answered any incorrectly), and (2) participants were asked whether the speaker in the video stimulus was wearing long sleeves (and were excluded if they answered more than half of the trials incorrectly).
Before the 12 experimental trials, participants filled out a demographic survey.
Not surprisingly (Revsine et al., 2025), participants were consistent in the stimuli they remembered when presented auditorily (Spearman-Brown corrected, SBc, ρ=.67, p<.001; Fig. 3B).
But participants were also consistent in the stimuli they remembered when presented visually (SBc ρ=.49, p<.001, Fig. 3A) and audiovisually (SBc ρ=.59, p<.001, Fig. 3C).
Between 32% and 45% of the recruited online participants were excluded, which aligns with current exclusion rates for online experiments.

Speakers naturally move their hands when they talk--they gesture.
These co-speech gestures serve communication by giving listeners access to information, some of which is found exclusively in gesture (Goldin-Meadow, 2003 , 2023).
text.formatted: These co-speech gestures serve communication by giving listeners access to information, some of which is found exclusively in gesture <ref type="bibr">(Goldin-Meadow, 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a speaker says, "I ran upstairs," while producing an upward spiral gesture; only the gesture tells the listener that the stairway is spiral.
Co-speech gesture is a unique visual stimulus because it is fully integrated with speech (Congdon et al., 2017; McNeill, 1992) and thus multimodal.
text.formatted: Co-speech gesture is a unique visual stimulus because it is fully integrated with speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Congdon et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">McNeill, 1992)</ref> and thus multimodal.

text.text: It is produced without speakers' intentional planning (Rauscher et al., 1996), reduces speakers' cognitive load (Goldin-Meadow et al., 2001; Ping & Goldin-Meadow, 2010), and benefits learning in speakers (Goldin-Meadow et al., 2009) and listeners (Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It is produced without speakers' intentional planning <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Rauscher et al., 1996)</ref>, reduces speakers' cognitive load <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Goldin-Meadow et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Ping & Goldin-Meadow, 2010)</ref>, and benefits learning in speakers <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Goldin-Meadow et al., 2009)</ref> and listeners <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Wang et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Zhang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These properties make gesture a powerful tool for teaching and learning.
However, the mechanisms underlying gesture's benefits are poorly understood, limiting its application to educational settings.
Gesture might affect learning by enhancing memory.

Although we know that gesture promotes memory for new vocabulary (So et al., 2012) and that information in speech is better remembered when it occurs with gesture than without it (Church et al., 2007), very little is known about how gesture affects memory.

text.text: Studies of visual stimuli other than gesture find that certain visual stimuli are more likely to be remembered than others, regardless of who is doing the remembering.

Despite individual differences in memory capability and personal experience, as a group, people tend to consistently remember, and forget, particular visual stimuli (Bainbridge et al., 2013; Guo & Bainbridge, 2025; Isola et al., 2011).

text.text: Such memory consistency across people for a given stimulus is called memorability.
Here, we examine whether people display memory consistency for co-speech gestures, presented with speech (gesture+speech audiovisual stimuli) and without it (gesture visual stimuli).
Importantly, only one prior study has studied memorability for multimodal stimuli, specifically examining audio and visual features of movie clips at a coarse level (Cohendet et al., 2018).

text.text: The close coupling between gesture and speech allows us to explore multimodal factors that shape memorability of audiovisual stimuli, as in everyday communication.

Studying memorability of gesture-speech stimuli, whose modalities are tightly integrated before encoding (Murray et al., 2024), can provide insight into the cognitive model of multisensory memory processing.

text.text: In Baddeley's (2020) influential model of working memory, auditory and visual information are processed separately and then integrated in an episodic buffer before being transferred to long-term memory.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Baddeley's (2020)</ref> influential model of working memory, auditory and visual information are processed separately and then integrated in an episodic buffer before being transferred to long-term memory.

text.text: This account allows for integration of information from separate modalities in the buffer, which could result in new information.

Importantly, Baddeley's model argues that the central executive, including attention, is not necessary for multisensory integration in the episodic buffer; that is, unisensory information can directly contribute to the episodic buffer without the central executive actively selecting and binding unisensory inputs.

In contrast, the predictive coding framework (Quak et al., 2015) suggests that attention plays a key role in determining what and how multimodal sensory inputs are combined with existing representations in long-term memory.

text.text: Memorability is well suited to disentangle the role of attention in memory for multimodal information because it explains variance in memory independent of attention (Wakeland-Hart et al., 2022).

text.text: But if gesture-speech integration takes place in the episodic memory buffer, where attentional control is not necessary, we might expect effects on memorability.
Finding that combined gesture-speech memorability exceeds what can be accounted for by gesture and speech memorability alone would provide additional evidence for Baddeley's (2020) buffer.

Memorability is driven by properties intrinsic to the stimulus, as found in thousands of participants remembering and forgetting the same stimuli across retrieval delays (Goetschalckx et al., 2018; Isola et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2021).

text.text: The speech+gesture stimuli we use offer an opportunity to examine how gesture's meaning and form, taken in relation to speech, affect memorability.

Here, we examined (1) whether certain gestures, presented alone or with speech, are more memorable than others, and, if so, (2) which properties of co-speech gesture (form/meaning) contribute to its memorability.

We ran a series of experiments to measure memorability of hundreds of stimuli presented to different participants in three conditions-gesture alone (visualonly), speech alone (audio-only), or gesture+speech together (visual+audio)-and we examined how they relate to each other.
To enhance the ecological validity of our stimuli, we used recordings of spontaneously produced gestures during speakers' explanations of a difficult concept.

text.text: We created a set of stimuli by video recording 20 naïve participants (whom we call "speakers"; see Supplemental Table .1.1 for information on the speakers and Supplemental Method.1 for methods used to generate and process the video recordings).

Overview of the Method for Stimulus Creation and the Memory Test Note.
During stimulus creation stage, we video-recorded 20 adults (denoted as "speakers" for clarity) explaining Piagetian liquid conservation problems using unscripted speech and gestures.
These audiovisual recordings were processed into visual-only (gesture) and audio-only (speech) stimuli, and we extracted gesture and speech features from them.

During the memory test stage with new participants, we collected memorability data for each stimulus by running online participants in a study/test recognition memory task, using a between-subjects design.
We selected 18 10-second explanation snippets from each of the 20 adult speakers.
The 10-second duration was chosen because it is sufficient time to capture an entire gesture and to avoid extended speech pauses.
Each snippet could start or end in the middle of a sentence, but it contained sensible speech information relevant to conservation.
We thus created 360 audiovisual stimuli containing gestures and speech.
To obtain a corresponding set of visual-only stimuli with gesture but not speech, we muted the 360 audiovisual stimuli.

To obtain a corresponding set of audio-only stimuli with speech but not gesture, we extracted the soundtrack of each audiovisual stimulus and paired it with a neutral-posed (sitting with hands on laps) static image of the speaker who produced the soundtrack.
See an example audiovisual stimulus, and its corresponding visual-only and audio-only stimuli at https://osf.io/uxzve/overview?view_only=4ac185e124fc4c4086ec802996c0ccd5.

text.text: We recruited 1338, 1165, and 1545 online participants using Prolific for the audiovisual, visual-only, and audio-only experiments, respectively.
To ensure data quality, we only recruited participants who reported being fluent English speakers in the United States and having at least 90% approval rates on at least 50 previous tasks.

After applying our exclusion criteria (see Section II.C), we were left with the following number of participants for each experiment: (1) 799 for audiovisual (400 female, 372 male, 27 other; mean age = 40.33, age range = [18,94]); (2) 787 for visual-only (429 female, 329 male, 29 other; mean age = 38.12, age range = [18,78]); (3) 851 for audio-only (452 female, 360 male, 39 other; mean age = 35.90, age range = [18,74]).

Each stimulus was viewed by about 40 participants, as prior work shows that memorability scores can be sufficiently calculated from 40 viewers (Isola et al., 2014; see Supplemental Table.2.1 for number of participants assigned to each speaker).
Each experiment took approximately sixteen minutes.
For all online experiments in this study, participants were compensated an hourly rate of $8.00 and were allowed to end the experiment at any time.
All participants consented to participate following the Institutional Review Board (IRB) guidelines at University of Chicago (IRB98-056, IRB19-1395, applied to all experiments in this study).

The memory test consisted of two blocks with the same study-test design.
During the study phase in block 1, nine random stimuli (each 10-seconds long) from a randomly chosen speaker (Speaker 1) were each presented with a 1-second fixation cross in between.

During the test phase that followed a page of test instructions, 18 stimuli from the same speaker (Speaker 1) were presented in 18 trials, and participants were asked to rate whether each stimulus was new or old on a 5-point Likert scale.
Block 2 was the same as block 1, except that the encoding and testing stimuli came from another randomly chosen speaker (Speaker 2).
Participants' memory test performance was used to measure stimulus memorability.
Speakers wore face shields to protect their identities and to eliminate communicative cues conveyed through facial expressions and lip movements.
Before proceeding with the online task, participants answered prescreening questions to ensure that the video and sound would play smoothly.

In the audiovisual experiment, participants answered a video prescreening question that required them to count and report the number of letters within a digit sequence, and an audio prescreening question that required them to type out a sentence they had heard.
Participants could replay the video and audio.
Participants in the visual-only experiment answered only the video prescreening question, and participants in the audio-only experiment answered only the audio prescreening question.
The online task used a study-test paradigm (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: The online task used a study-test paradigm (Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Each participant was randomly assigned to observe two speakers in two different study-test blocks of the experiment.
During the study phase, 9 stimuli (a random half of stimuli associated with a speaker) were presented in a sequence with a 1-s interstimulus interval during which a fixation cross appeared.
Participants were not provided with any context for the speakers' explanations and were instructed to memorize the 9 stimuli for an upcoming memory test.
As an attention check, the border of each stimulus turned red at a random time point during the last three seconds of each trial as the stimulus was playing.
Participants were told to press the r key when the border turned red.
Regardless of whether participants indicated the red border, it disappeared at the end of each trial.

After the study phase, participants were shown instructions for the test phase, and their memory was tested using 18 old/new memory judgment test trials that included the 9 studied stimuli and 9 foil stimuli from the same speaker.
In each test trial, the stimulus was presented in a looped manner, and the participant had to rate the stimulus as "definitely old," "probably old," "not sure," "probably new," or "definitely new."
An optional break followed the first study-test block.
The second study-test block was the same as the first, except that stimuli from another randomly chosen speaker were presented.
At the end of the second study-test block, participants filled out a demographic survey, rated whether the experiment ran smoothly, and gave additional comments, if any.

We chose the study-test paradigm for two reasons: (1) We wanted to test memory within the same speaker's gestures to avoid extraneous differences between speakers (e.g., backgrounds, clothes) that might affect participants' memory.

(2) There were not enough stimuli (18/speaker) to serve as targets and fillers in a continuous recognition paradigm (a more commonly used paradigm to test memorability), where participants indicate target repeats within a stimulus sequence containing targets and fillers.

Memorability has been shown to be a robust measure across different task parameters (Bainbridge, 2020; Bylinskii et al., 2015; Goetschalckx et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2020), and extends to the study-test paradigm (e.g., Gillies et al., 2023; Goetschalckx et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2020).

text.text: Expert-coded semantic meaning of gesture and speech.
We adapted a system developed to code children's speech and gesture explanations of their beliefs about conservation (Church & Goldin-Meadow, 1986).
text.formatted: We adapted a system developed to code children's speech and gesture explanations of their beliefs about conservation <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Church & Goldin-Meadow, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Table .2 lists the strategies the speakers gave, divided into five types (dimensions, identity, count-equate, add-subtract, actions), with examples of each strategy in gesture and in speech.
Two trained experimenters coded independently, focusing on a single modality each time, and discussed disagreements to make final coding decisions.

Intercoder reliabilities (IR) for gesture strategies and speech strategies were 80.17% and 80.34%, respectively, established using different stimuli subsets (each subset contained 15% of the 360 stimuli, coming from at least 6 different speakers).
When an overarching strategy contained component strategies (e.g., Compensation contains Height-Comparison and Width-Comparison), the overarching strategy was coded rather than the components.

The speakers often produced different strategies in speech and gesture within a single explanation (see Church & Goldin-Meadow, 1986); as a result, the speech and gesture strategies within a stimulus may differ.

text.text: Our experts also coded visual form features in gesture, which predicted memory patterns in gesture (see Supplemental Results.5); however, because we can test gesture form with greater subtlety using motion tracking (see next subsection), we focus on the meaning coding our experts did and not their form coding.

We operationalized semantic meaning as the number of unique strategies represented in a snippet to capture a measure of informativeness in each modality (see Supplemental Results.4 for analyses suggesting that no single gesture or speech strategy predicted gesture memorability).
The number of gesture strategies within a stimulus ranged from 0 to 5, and the number of speech strategies within a stimulus ranged from 0 to 4.

We counted the number of strategies that appeared uniquely in gesture (i.e., in gesture and not in speech) in each of the 360 stimuli, as well as the number of strategies that appeared uniquely in speech (i.e., in speech and not gesture).
We also examined the effects of speech informativeness on gesture memorability because the informativeness of gesture and speech modalities has been shown to be related (Cánovas et al., 2020).

Computationally extracted visual form features of gesture.

For each 10-second video stimulus (≈ 30 fps), we extracted Cartesian coordinate landmarks of the left and right wrists in 29 (evenly-spaced) frames using Google MediaPipe, an open-source computer vision tool that tracks hand movements in the vertical, horizontal, and depth dimensions (Lugaresi et al., 2019).
text.formatted: For each 10-second video stimulus (≈ 30 fps), we extracted Cartesian coordinate landmarks of the left and right wrists in 29 (evenly-spaced) frames using Google MediaPipe, an open-source computer vision tool that tracks hand movements in the vertical, horizontal, and depth dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Lugaresi et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The extracted wrist landmarks were meter (unit) estimations of real-world coordinates from the origin (the midpoint of the speakers' hips).
Based on the wrist coordinate data, we computed parameters that quantified the visual form features of gestures.
For each video stimulus, we measured parameters related to 8 broad categories of features used to characterize the distance, speed, and other aspects of gestures (Table .3).
For each form category, we extracted its mean and standard deviation on three dimensions (vertical, horizontal, and depth) for the left, right, and both wrists combined (See Supplemental Method.7).
We generated 154 parameters, including 87 distance-related parameters, 45 speed-related parameters, and 22 other parameters.

Naïve online crowdsourced ratings of meaning, form, and other features of gesture.
To examine how naïve viewers judged the gesture movements, we collected non-expert judgments of movement-related features for visual-only stimuli.

We recruited a new group of 472 online participants on Prolific (221 female, 204 male, 27 other, see Supplemental Table.8.2 for age composition) and asked them to rate 12 attributes on a nine-point Likert scale (1=not at all,9=extremely) for gestures in each visual-only stimulus.

The list of gesture-related features was adapted from prior work on dance memorability (Ongchoco et al., 2022): three subjective taste features (beauty, emotion, interest), five movement-related features (simplicity, speed, energy, scale, difficulty to produce), and three memory-related features (typicality, familiarity, subjective memorability judgment).
text.formatted: The list of gesture-related features was adapted from prior work on dance memorability <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ongchoco et al., 2022)</ref>: three subjective taste features (beauty, emotion, interest), five movement-related features (simplicity, speed, energy, scale, difficulty to produce), and three memory-related features (typicality, familiarity, subjective memorability judgment).

text.text: We added a 12 th feature, a meaning-related feature (understandability), for this task.
Each participant was asked to rate 12 random visual-only stimuli, resulting in an average of fourteen ratings per attribute per visual-only stimulus.
The experiment took approximately fifteen minutes.

To help clarify the 12 features for the participants, antonyms of the features (e.g., understandable versus confusing) were listed, and dictionary definitions of the features were provided in a pop-up window (see Supplemental Method.8).

Each trial (rating of 12 attributes on 1 visual-only stimulus) contained two attention check questions: (1) participants were asked to indicate a computer-generated random number between 1 and 9 (and were excluded if they answered any incorrectly), and (2) participants were asked whether the speaker in the video stimulus was wearing long sleeves (and were excluded if they answered more than half of the trials incorrectly).
We excluded 45 participants upon applying these exclusion criteria (25 failed criterion (1), 19 failed (2), and 1 failed both), resulting in 472 valid participants.

Although all 12 stimuli were new to participants, they might have mistakenly believed they had seen a stimulus before, either because they saw the same speaker or because all speakers gestured about liquid conservation.

To minimize familiarity effects on naïve ratings, we excluded 257 trials (but not participants) in which participants reported having previously seen the video, resulting in 5167 valid trials across the 472 valid participants.
Before the 12 experimental trials, participants filled out a demographic survey.
For each visual-only stimulus, we calculated averaged ratings across participants on each of the 12 features, indicating naïve non-experts' perception of speakers' gestures.
The average feature ratings range from 1 to 9.

We removed multicollinear features (|r| > .7), making sure to include scale of movements because this feature significantly predicts memorability of dance moves, a dynamic visual stimulus (Ongchoco et al., 2022) that might show similarities to gesture.

text.text: We thus analyzed crowdsourced ratings for 6 features: scale of movement, beauty, difficulty to produce, typicality, familiarity, and understandability.

text.text: Our first question is whether memorability extends to gesture, with speech or without it.

To determine whether there are consistent memory patterns across people for our gesture and speech stimuli, we tested split-half reliability of hit rate, HR (Supplemental Method.2), for 360 stimuli presented in visual-only (M=.60, SD=.12), audio-only (M=.72, SD=.12), and audiovisual (M=.69, SD=.12) conditions.
Not surprisingly (Revsine et al., 2025), participants were consistent in the stimuli they remembered when presented auditorily (Spearman-Brown corrected, SBc, ρ=.67, p<.001; Fig. 3B).
text.formatted: Not surprisingly <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Revsine et al., 2025)</ref>, participants were consistent in the stimuli they remembered when presented auditorily (Spearman-Brown corrected, SBc, ρ=.67, p<.001; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3B</ref>).

text.text: But participants were also consistent in the stimuli they remembered when presented visually (SBc ρ=.49, p<.001, Fig. 3A) and audiovisually (SBc ρ=.59, p<.001, Fig. 3C).

text.text: Certain gestures, presented with or without speech, are better remembered than others across people.
This is the first robust evidence that multimodal stimuli show consistent memory patterns across populations.
To examine whether gesture+speech memorability is predicted by memorability of its unimodal components, we ran Spearman correlations across conditions for all 360 stimuli.

text.text: However, the interaction between audio-only HR and visual-only HR was significant (β=.13, p=.05), suggesting that the effect of gesture on audiovisual memory depends on its accompanying speech.
To explore this interaction, we grouped stimuli into low-, medium-, and high-audio HR tertiles (120 stimuli each) and correlated visual-only and audiovisual HRs within each tertile.
Visual-only HR correlated with audiovisual HR when audio-only HR was high (Spearman ρ=.23, p=.01), but not when it was low or medium (ps>.05) (Fig. 5).

text.text: Therefore, memorability of audiovisual (speech+gesture) stimuli is affected by memorability of its visual component (gesture) only if its audio component (speech) is highly memorable.
Speech memorability influences whether the accompanying gesture is memorable.

Feature analysis results in the following sections (III.C-E) are similar when the same analyses are conducted using the 120 stimuli with high-audio HR (see Supplemental Results.6); we therefore focused on the full set of 360 stimuli for the feature analyses.
We conducted the reverse analysis, grouping stimuli into low-, medium-, and high-visual HR tertiles (120 each).
Audio-only HR correlated with audiovisual HR for low (ρ=.46, p<.001), medium (ρ=.71, p<.001) and high (ρ=.60, p<.001) visual-only tertiles.

text.text: However, the correlation was significantly stronger in medium than low visual-only HR tertiles (Fisher's z=-2.98, p=.001, one-tailed); medium and high tertiles did not differ significantly.
Therefore, memorability of audiovisual stimuli is more affected by memorability of its audio component (speech) if its visual component (gesture) is more memorable.
Thus, gesture memorability also influences whether the accompanying speech is memorable.
Finally, we wanted to test whether there was a remaining memorability effect of the integrated audiovisual stimuli when taking out its separate audio and visual memorability components.

To examine this question, we tested the residuals from the linear regression, which represent the portion of the stimulus' audiovisual HR that cannot be explained by a linear combination of its visual-only and audio-only HR.
A split-half consistency analysis on the residuals (Supplemental Method.2) showed significant cross-participant consistency (360 stimuli: SBc ρ=.31, p=.001, Fig. 3D).

text.text: As expected, the residuals from the 360 stimuli did not correlate with visual-only or audio-only HR (ps>.05), suggesting that the multimodal residuals capture information beyond the information in either modality.

text.text: Audiovisual memorability thus reflects a whole that is more than the sum of its unimodal components--integrating auditory and visual information produces new information that participants consistently latch onto.
What features account for gesture memorability?
We focus first on meaning categories coded in gesture (Table .2).
Number of gesture strategies positively predicted visual-only HR (Spearman ρ=.17, p<.001), suggesting that more informative gestures (those containing more strategies) were better remembered.

text.text: The total number of gestures did not predict visual-only HR (p>.05), suggesting that more memorable gestures are not simply those containing more individual gestures, but rather those containing more information.

text.text: Interestingly, when gesture was embedded in speech in the audiovisual condition, number of gesture strategies did not predict audiovisual HR (p>.05).

text.text: We controlled for the number of gestures and found that the total number of gestures did predict audiovisual HR (Spearman's ρ=.12, p=.02), suggesting that participants attend to individual gestures more when gesture is embedded in speech but without extracting more meaning from them.
Because speech and gesture were produced simultaneously, speech information might have affected information conveyed in gestures.
We therefore conducted the same analyses on speech meaning categories.
As expected, number of speech strategies positively predicted audiovisual HR (Spearman ρ=.18, p<.001).

text.text: We then modeled how much variability in visual-only HR could be accounted for by strategies unique to each modality and shared across modalities.
The model fit was significant (adjusted R² =.04, p<.001, AIC=571).

text.text: We modeled the same linear regression to predict audiovisual HR, and found a significant model fit (adjusted R² =.02, p=.01, AIC=698).
Speech-unique (β=.13, p=.005) and shared (β=.14, p=.02) strategies significantly predicted audiovisual memorability, but gesture-unique strategies did not (p>.05).

text.text: To the extent that gesture meaning influences audiovisual memorability, it is when gesture and speech convey the same information.
We first examined gesture form independent of meaning.
We correlated each of the 154 visual form parameters (standardized), extracted using computer vision, with visual-only HR and audiovisual HR.
We found no significant correlations with False Discovery Rate correction (q<.05, ps>.05).

text.text: We then asked whether form features that reflect meaningful distinctions on the task predict gesture memorability.
Because the dimensions of the containers in the task are crucial for understanding conservation, we examined distance-related form features, contrasting them with speed-related features.
We fitted separate linear regressions to predict visual-only and audiovisual HR using 87 distance-related parameters, and we fitted separate linear regressions using 45 speed-related parameters.

We used stepwise linear regression to avoid making assumptions about parameter collinearity for two reasons: (1) there are no psychological theories specifying how these parameters are conceptually related within the visual system; (2) we included the same parameters for left, right, and both wrists combined, which are inherently correlated.
Using distance-related parameters to predict visual-only HR led to significant model fit (adjusted R² =.02, p=.01, AIC=574).
Using speed-related parameters did not (p>.05).
text.formatted: Using speed-related parameters did not (p>.05).

text.text: We found the same results for audiovisual HR (distance-related: adjusted R² =.05, p<.001, AIC=687; speedrelated: p>.05).
text.formatted: We found the same results for audiovisual HR (distance-related: adjusted R² =.05, p<.001, AIC=687; speedrelated: p>.05).

text.text: Gesture lengths and distances, which are related to reasoning about conservation, better predict gesture memorability (with or without speech) than gesture speed and manner, which are not directly related to reasoning about conservation.
The finding adds to the gesture literature by reinforcing the practice of focusing on gesture meaning, rather than form, to predict learning (Goldin-Meadow, 2003).

text.text: To explore whether gesture meaning and form together contribute to its memorability, we ran a stepwise linear regression model to predict visual-only HR (logit-transformed) using both number of gesture strategies (a meaning feature; standardized) and 154 visual parameters (all form features, including distance-and speed-related features; standardized) as predictors.

We found significant model fit (adjusted R² =.04, p<.001, AIC=568), with number of gesture strategies (β=.09, p<.001) and a distance-related form feature (SDvertical hand distance; β=-.07, p=.02) as significant predictors of visual-only HR.

We found several distance-related features (scale, magnitude, distance between hands on vertical/sagittal dimensions) and a direction feature to be significant predictors (adjusted R² =.06, p<.001, AIC=687; Supplemental Table .7.1), but not number of gesture strategies.

text.text: Only gesture's distance-related form features (which are related to meaning) predict both visual-only and audiovisual memorability.
We examined the impact of ratings by non-experts on gesture memorability.
Using naïve ratings of visual-only stimuli, we conducted separate linear regressions to predict visual-only and audiovisual HR (see Supplemental Table .8.3 for descriptive statistics).

The model predicting visual-only HR was marginally significant (p=.06, Table .4), indicating that the gesture features examined-including scale of movement, which reliably predicts memorability in dance (Ongchoco et al., 2022)-do not predict memorability when gesture is presented without speech.
text.formatted: The model predicting visual-only HR was marginally significant (p=.06, Table .4), indicating that the gesture features examined-including scale of movement, which reliably predicts memorability in dance <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ongchoco et al., 2022)</ref>-do not predict memorability when gesture is presented without speech.

text.text: The model predicting audiovisual HR was significant (adjusted R² =.03, p=.01, AIC=699).
In both models, gesture typicality was the only significant predictor (visual-only: β=.08, p=.02; audiovisual: β=.11, p=.008).

We found the same pattern when using naïve ratings of audiovisual stimuli from a separate group, suggesting that the limited predictive power of these naïve ratings was not due to the absence of speech (Supplemental Results.9, Tables.8.1-.2,8.4,9.1).
Our study has three central findings.
First, we provide the first robust evidence that multimodal stimuli elicit consistent memory patterns across individuals.
In other words, the memorability effect extends to multimodal stimuli--in particular, to gestures spontaneously produced with speech.
Our findings thus extend memorability to a multimodal behavior naturally produced in everyday settings.
Second, we show that memorability for multimodal stimuli is explained by distinct contributions of its unimodal information streams.
Memorability of gesture+speech is predicted by gesture memorability (on its own) only when the accompanying speech is highly memorable (on its own).
Memorability of gesture+speech is also better predicted by speech memorability (on its own) when the accompanying gesture is more memorable (on its own).
But memorability for multimodal stimuli is also explained by integrated information across the unimodal streams.
Participants consistently remembered aspects of the audiovisual stimuli not explained by memory for the visual-only or audio-only versions.

Audiovisual memorability thus reflects a whole that is more than the simple combination of its unimodal parts--integrating auditory and visual information produces additional information, reliably remembered across people.

The fact that gesture-speech memorability goes beyond the independent contributions of gesture memorability and speech memorability provides support for the episodic buffer in Baddeley's (2020) model.
According to the model, auditory and visual (in this case, speech and gesture) information are processed separately and integrated within the buffer before being transferred to long-term memory.
The buffer allows for additional information to be created by providing a stage when information from the individual sensory modalities can be integrated.

Because memorability explains variance in memory independent of attentional factors (Wakeland-Hart et al., 2022), the fact that memorability for gesture+speech goes beyond its component parts suggests that memory, rather than attention, is central to gesture-speech integration.
text.formatted: Because memorability explains variance in memory independent of attentional factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Wakeland-Hart et al., 2022)</ref>, the fact that memorability for gesture+speech goes beyond its component parts suggests that memory, rather than attention, is central to gesture-speech integration.

text.text: Under Baddeley's (2020) model, working-memory resources are limited and shared across processing modules.
When encoding speech on its own, auditory processing receives all available resources, and when encoding gesture on its own, visual processing receives all available resources.
During gesture-speech encoding, if the visual module requires fewer resources to process gesture, more resources become available to the auditory module (and vice versa).

Because more memorable stimuli require less time and fewer resources to encode (Bainbridge et al., 2026), memorable speech or gesture may reduce a listener's cognitive load, leaving more resources available to process the other modality or integrate the two modalities.
text.formatted: Because more memorable stimuli require less time and fewer resources to encode <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bainbridge et al., 2026)</ref>, memorable speech or gesture may reduce a listener's cognitive load, leaving more resources available to process the other modality or integrate the two modalities.

text.text: Our findings align with this prediction: gesture memorability predicted gesture-speech memorability only when speech was highly memorable, and speech memorability was more strongly correlated with audiovisual memorability when gesture was more memorable.

Hostetter (2011) also found that gesture has the greatest impact on learning and memory when it conveys clear, unambiguous information not present in speech, suggesting that informative gestures, which are likely to be memorable, enhance memory for gesture-speech communication.
These findings shed light on how gesture could benefit learning.
Third, we find that gesture memorability is predicted by its meaning.
The number of strategies found uniquely in gesture, as well as the number shared across gesture and speech-but not the number of individual gestures--predict gesture memorability.

Moreover, to the extent that visual form features predict memorability, it is the features capturing dimensions relevant to the task that have an impact on memorability, again suggesting that memorability for gesture is based on meaning.
These findings highlight differences across different types of dynamic visual information.

Because co-speech gestures are inherently meaningful and convey messages to listeners (e.g., Goldin-Meadow & Sandhofer, 1999), it is not surprising that listeners remember gestures based on semantic meaning, rather than visual form.
text.formatted: Because co-speech gestures are inherently meaningful and convey messages to listeners (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Goldin-Meadow & Sandhofer, 1999)</ref>, it is not surprising that listeners remember gestures based on semantic meaning, rather than visual form.

text.text: Nor is it surprising that visual features had an impact on gesture memorability only when highlighting a meaningful strategy.
In contrast, dance movements are not necessarily intended to be interpreted semantically, and their memorability is predicted by visual form (movement scale, Ongchoco et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In contrast, dance movements are not necessarily intended to be interpreted semantically, and their memorability is predicted by visual form (movement scale, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ongchoco et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, in narrative-based dance forms-such as Indian classical dances or musical theater choreography-meaning might also contribute to memorability.

Future research is needed on dynamic visual stimuli that vary in meaning, and on cases in which the same stimulus affords different levels of meaningful parsing across individuals (e.g., sign language comprehension in fluent signers versus naïve viewers).
It is, of course, possible that the distance-related form features isolated here are memorable in other contexts.
The finding that "typicality" predicts memorability in the naïve ratings study could mean that distance forms are recognizable as typical and therefore memorable regardless of task.
To be certain that gesture form impacts memorability only through meaning, we need to conduct our study with tasks that give rise to gestures with different forms.
Nevertheless, our study provides support for the hypothesis that coding gesture meaning is more important than coding gesture form when assessing gesture's impact on cognition (Goldin-Meadow, 2003).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, our study provides support for the hypothesis that coding gesture meaning is more important than coding gesture form when assessing gesture's impact on cognition <ref type="bibr">(Goldin-Meadow, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: And, as our study shows, gesture needs to be coded and analyzed in relation to the speech it accompanies to fully determine its impact.
Our study investigates the memorability of naturally elicited, multimodal stimuli and demonstrates how the constituent modalities interact to contribute to overall memorability.
We also discovered that semantic meaning features are the driving force behind gesture memorability in our task.
Visual form features predict gesture memorability only when they reflect the semantics of the task.
Interestingly, these visual features become even more important to memorability when the same gestures are presented with speech.
Overall, this study opens a new direction for examining memory for dynamic, multimodal stimuli and offers a methodological framework for isolating unimodal contributions within complex stimuli.

Although decades of work show that gesture supports learning, the gap between gesture and cognitive research limits our understanding of mechanisms linking gesture to its behavioral benefits (see Guo et al., 2025, for review).
text.formatted: Although decades of work show that gesture supports learning, the gap between gesture and cognitive research limits our understanding of mechanisms linking gesture to its behavioral benefits (see <ref type="bibr">Guo et al., 2025, for review)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, despite evidence that gestures aid learning in several domains (e.g., mathematics, conservation, chemistry), we still know little about which gesture properties affect memory and how they do so, making it difficult to harness gesture in classrooms.
This study provides the first attempt to probe memory mechanisms underlying gesture's benefits.

Our results reveal nuanced effects of different gesture properties-particularly in coordination with speech-highlighting the need for further research on cognitive processes that make gesture effective across contexts.

Notably, multimodal integration between gesture and speech generates new information not present in either modality alone, which people consistently latch onto and use to enrich representations held in memory.
A clearer understanding of these mechanisms will help educators and caregivers use gesture more effectively in real-world environments.
